questions.stem: In the Haber process, what are the raw materials used to make ammonia?

options.text: Nitrogen and oxygen
Nitrogen and hydrogen
Hydrogen and oxygen
Carbon dioxide and hydrogen

questions.explanation: The Haber process combines nitrogen (from the air) and hydrogen (from natural gas) to produce ammonia: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃.

questions.stem: The Haber process uses a temperature of about 450°C. Why is a higher temperature not used, even though it would increase the rate?

options.text: Higher temperatures would melt the catalyst
The forward reaction is exothermic, so a higher temperature would decrease the yield of ammonia
Higher temperatures are illegal in chemical plants
Higher temperatures would cause the nitrogen to decompose

questions.explanation: The forward reaction is exothermic, so increasing temperature shifts the equilibrium to the left, reducing the yield of ammonia. 450°C is a compromise between a reasonable rate and an acceptable yield.

questions.stem: Why is high pressure (about 200 atmospheres) used in the Haber process?

options.text: It makes the catalyst work better
There are fewer moles of gas on the product side, so high pressure shifts equilibrium to the right
It lowers the activation energy
It prevents the ammonia from decomposing

questions.explanation: The forward reaction produces fewer moles of gas (4 moles on the left vs 2 on the right). High pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules, shifting equilibrium to the right and increasing ammonia yield.

questions.stem: What is the role of the iron catalyst in the Haber process?

options.text: It increases the yield of ammonia
It speeds up the rate at which equilibrium is reached without changing the yield
It shifts the equilibrium to the right
It removes ammonia from the mixture

questions.explanation: The iron catalyst speeds up both the forward and reverse reactions equally, allowing equilibrium to be reached more quickly. It does not change the position of equilibrium or the yield.

questions.stem: What is meant by a 'compromise temperature' in industrial processes?

options.text: A temperature that gives the maximum possible yield
A temperature that balances an acceptable yield with a reasonable rate of reaction
The lowest temperature at which the reaction will occur
A temperature chosen to save money on cooling

questions.explanation: A compromise temperature is chosen to balance yield and rate. A lower temperature might give better yield but the reaction would be too slow, while a higher temperature gives faster rate but lower yield.

questions.stem: In the Contact process, what product is ultimately manufactured?

options.text: Ammonia
Nitric acid
Sulfuric acid
Hydrochloric acid

questions.explanation: The Contact process is the industrial method for manufacturing sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄), involving the catalytic oxidation of sulfur dioxide to sulfur trioxide.

questions.stem: Why do industrial processes often remove the product as soon as it forms in a reversible reaction?

options.text: To prevent the product from becoming too concentrated
Removing the product shifts the equilibrium to the right, producing more product
To reduce the pressure in the reaction vessel
To cool down the reaction mixture

questions.explanation: Removing the product decreases its concentration, which according to Le Chatelier's principle shifts the equilibrium to the right (towards making more product), improving the overall yield.
